Korean gugak, meaning national music, is the indigenous music tradition of Korea. It encompasses court music, folk instrumental pieces, and vocal traditions. Like other East Asian classical traditions, gugak emphasizes melodic subtlety, refined timbre, and the emotional expression of the performer. Ensemble and solo pieces showcase instruments uniquely Korean and often preserve musical styles lost in neighboring traditions.

Court music, called jeongak, includes ancient instrumental pieces such as sanjo and pansori alongside orchestral works performed at court and in contemporary concert halls. The tradition was nearly lost during Japanese occupation and has been actively revived in modern times. Primary instruments include the gayageum, a zither-like plucked instrument with twelve or more strings, and the geomungo, an angular zither played with a plectrum. The daegeum is a large transverse flute, while the janggu is a double-headed hourglass drum that provides rhythm and often takes solo turns.

Pansori is a particularly distinctive narrative vocal tradition where a single singer, accompanied only by a drummer, performs long epic tales with dramatic vocal effects and emotional intensity. It was designated UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in two thousand three. The sanjo form is an instrumental solo or small ensemble that begins slowly and accelerates rhythmically, resembling the alap-jor-jhala progression found in Hindustani music.

Gugak uses a five-note pentatonic scale similar to Chinese music, yet the microtonal bending and ornamentation are distinctly Korean, producing a unique timbral character. Rhythmic cycles called jangdan structure many pieces, and the janggu drummer is often a virtuoso soloist featured prominently in ensemble contexts. The Korean National Classical Music Institute and modern concert halls have established gugak as a living tradition. Contemporary composers now blend gugak with Western forms, ensuring its relevance to new audiences.
